back: A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a pathogen, with a specific shape that the body recognises as foreign.
A protein made by lymphocytes, with a shape complementary to one specific antigen, which binds to it.
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies.
Defence by antibodies made in the body itself after infection or vaccination; long-term, because memory cells are made.
Short-term defence by antibodies received from another individual (placenta, breast milk, antiserum); no memory cells.
They remain after an infection or vaccine and, on a later infection, make antibodies faster and in larger amounts.
Its antigens (weakened or dead pathogens) stimulate lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells without causing disease.

front: How does vaccinating many people control a disease?
back: Few people can catch and pass on the pathogen, so transmission chains break and unvaccinated people are protected too.
Natural active: infection. Artificial active: vaccine. Natural passive: placenta or breast milk. Artificial passive: antiserum such as antivenom.

front: Why use antiserum (e.g. antivenom) after a snake bite?
back: It contains ready-made antibodies that act immediately; a vaccine would take too long.
The Expanded Programme on Immunisation: free vaccines for children against diseases such as TB (BCG), polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and measles.

front: How does HIV weaken the immune system?
back: It destroys lymphocytes, so fewer antibodies are made and opportunistic infections such as TB develop.
